content: Currently, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of fluoroquinolones only for individuals with presumed drug-sensitive tuberculosis (TB) who are unable to tolerate standard first-line drugs. However, there is interest in exploring whether fluoroquinolones could potentially shorten the duration of treatment and improve outcomes in these patients. This review evaluates the effects of fluoroquinolones when used as part of first-line treatment regimens for drug-sensitive TB. The objective of this review was to assess the role of fluoroquinolones as either substitutes for or additions to standard antituberculous drug regimens in the treatment of drug-sensitive TB. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, the Science Citation Index, Russian publication databases, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials. The search included studies up to March 6, 2013. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated antituberculous regimens based on rifampicin and pyrazinamide, with fluoroquinolones either added to or substituted for other drugs in the regimen. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility of studies, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, and statistical analyses were performed using risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and a fixed-effect model when appropriate. Five RCTs involving a total of 1,330 participants met the inclusion criteria. None of these trials evaluated treatment regimens shorter than six months. 1. Fluoroquinolones added to standard regimens: One trial (174 participants) investigated the addition of levofloxacin to the standard first-line regimen. The trial did not report on relapse or treatment failure. For outcomes such as death, sputum conversion, and adverse events, the evidence was of very low quality, and it remains uncertain whether the addition of levofloxacin had any effect. 2. Fluoroquinolones substituted for ethambutol in standard regimens: Three trials (723 participants) substituted ethambutol with moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin, or ofloxacin in the standard first-line regimen. For relapse, the evidence was of very low quality, and it is uncertain whether there was any effect (one trial, 170 participants). None of the trials reported on treatment failure. For outcomes such as death, sputum culture conversion at eight weeks, and serious adverse events, the evidence was of very low quality, and it is unclear whether there was any effect. 3. Fluoroquinolones substituted for isoniazid in standard regimens: One trial (433 participants) substituted moxifloxacin for isoniazid in the standard regimen. The trial did not report on treatment failure or relapse. For outcomes such as death, sputum culture conversion, and serious adverse events, the substitution of moxifloxacin for isoniazid may have little or no difference (low-quality evidence). 4. Fluoroquinolones in four-month regimens: Six trials are currently ongoing to evaluate the use of fluoroquinolones in shorter treatment regimens lasting four months. Conclusions: Fluoroquinolones, including ofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and gatifloxacin, have been tested in RCTs as part of standard first-line regimens based on rifampicin and pyrazinamide for the treatment of drug-sensitive TB. However, the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether the addition or substitution of fluoroquinolones for ethambutol or isoniazid in these regimens reduces mortality, decreases relapse rates, or improves culture conversion at eight weeks. Larger trials investigating the use of fluoroquinolones in shorter four-month regimens are ongoing and may provide more definitive evidence in the future.
